title: Non-conventional slags as sustainable alternatives in concrete: a comprehensive review
abstract: Abstract Non-conventional slag (NCS), including copper, lead, lithium, nickel, phosphorus, and zinc slags are under-utilised industrial by-products with potential in sustainable construction. This review evaluates their use as partial replacements for cement and aggregates, focusing on performance and mechanisms. NCS behaviour varies with composition and activation, with some enhancing strength and durability. Most importantly, NCS supports waste valorisation, reduced material consumption, and more sustainable concrete development.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The construction industry is one of the largest consumers of natural resources, accounting for nearly 40% of global energy consumption and 50% of greenhouse gas emissions 1 , 2 . This vast environmental footprint emphasises the need for sustainable alternatives to traditional construction materials. The United Nations’ 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development set forth 17 sustainable development goals (SDGs), six of which are directly relevant to the construction industry: SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation), SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy), SDG 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure), SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities), SDG 12 (responsible consumption and production), and SDG 13 (climate action) 3 . Reducing the environmental impact of cement and concrete production through the utilisation of industrial by-products has therefore become an important strategy for achieving these sustainability objectives.

Among the various industrial by-products, ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS) and steel slag (SS) have been widely used as supplementary cementitious materials or aggregate substitutes in cement-based materials 4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 . GGBS is well known for improving concrete durability and long-term strength 8 , while SS has found widespread use in road construction due to its mechanical strength and abrasion resistance construction 9 . However, the long-term availability of GGBS is expected to decline in some regions due to the gradual reduction in blast furnace ironmaking and the growing demand for alternative supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) 10 . At the same time, the utilisation of SS in cementitious systems remains limited by factors such as volumetric instability, free CaO or MgO content, and variability in chemical composition. Consequently, increasing attention has been directed toward identifying alternative industrial by-products that can complement or partially replace conventional slags. One promising solution lies in non-conventional slag (NCS), which are produced as by-products from various industrial processes, including copper smelting, nickel refining, lead processing, phosphorus production, and lithium production. These slags are not widely utilised in construction and is not yet included in established material specifications for building materials, despite being generated in substantial quantities, and often result in environmental issues related to landfilling and waste management.

Despite their potential as alternative resources in cement-based materials, the practical utilisation of many NCS remains limited. Several barriers contribute to this situation. The chemical composition and mineralogical structure of NCS can vary significantly depending on ore sources and processing conditions, leading to uncertainty in their performance in cementitious systems. In addition, some NCS contain high MgO contents, phosphate compounds, or trace heavy metals, which may affect hydration behaviour, durability, or environmental safety. Furthermore, many NCS exhibit lower intrinsic reactivity than conventional SCMs, often requiring additional pre-treatment processes such as grinding or activation to achieve adequate performance. The absence of standardised guidelines further limits their widespread adoption in construction practice. Numerous experimental studies have investigated individual types of NCS and demonstrated their potential use as cementitious materials, fillers, or aggregate replacements in cement-based systems 11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 . Correspondingly, several review papers have been published focusing on specific slag types or particular metallurgical by-products. However, these studies are typically limited to single-material systems or narrow categories of industrial slags, making it difficult to obtain a comprehensive understanding of how different NCS compare in terms of their characteristics, reactivity, and engineering performance 13 , 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 . As research progresses and these materials prove their effectiveness, there is potential for NCS to be integrated into future material specifications and guidelines for more resource-efficient and sustainable construction practices.

sections.heading: Overview, scope of work, and methodology
paragraphs: This review critically evaluates the potential use of NCS, particularly non-ferrous slag (NFS) that includes copper slag (CS), lead slag (LDS), lithium slag (LTS), nickel slag (NS), phosphorus slag (PS), and zinc slag (ZS), as substitutes for cement and aggregates (both fine and coarse) in cement mortar and concrete. The study focuses on research published over the past two decades, reflecting the increasing interest in valorising industrial by-products for sustainable construction.

The review first discusses the generation and production processes of various NCS types, followed by a comparative assessment of their physical, chemical, and mineralogical properties. Particular emphasis is placed on understanding how these characteristics influence the mechanical performance and microstructural behaviour of cement-based materials when NCS are incorporated as SCMs or as replacements for natural aggregates.

In addition, the review examines different activation approaches, including mechanical, chemical, and thermal activation, which have been proposed to enhance the reactivity and performance of NCS in cementitious systems. The scope of this study is limited to the utilisation of NCS in conventional cement-based materials, including cement mortar and concrete. Applications of NCS in alkali-activated materials or geopolymer systems are excluded, as these systems involve fundamentally different binder chemistries and reaction mechanisms that fall beyond the scope of this review. By synthesising findings from a large body of published research, this review provides a comprehensive understanding of the current state of NCS research and its implications for sustainable construction practices. The findings of this study contribute to the broader field of sustainable concrete production, highlighting the critical role that under-utilised materials like NCS can play in reducing the construction industry’s environmental impact and supporting global sustainability goals.

To provide an overview of the distribution of existing research, the studies included in this review were further categorised according to the types of cement-based materials investigated. The resulting distribution is illustrated in Fig.  1 , which presents a heatmap summarising the number of studies on the utilisation of NCS across cement mortar and different concrete types. These include mortar (M), conventional concrete (CC), self-compacting concrete (SCC), high-strength/performance concrete (HSC), recycled coarse aggregate concrete (RCAC), reinforced concrete (RC), steel fibre-reinforced concrete (SFC), pervious concrete (PC), and lightweight recycled aggregate concrete (LRAC). The heatmap provides a visual representation of research trends and highlights areas where NCS applications have been more extensively studied, as well as areas that remain relatively underexplored. sections.heading: Generation and production of NCS
paragraphs: Table  1  summarises the generation routes of these NCS, while Fig.  2  illustrates the typical metallurgical processes involved in their formation. The extraction of non-ferrous metals generally involves several stages, including beneficiation, roasting, smelting, converting, and refining, depending on the metal type and ore composition. During smelting, ores are processed with fluxing agents to separate molten metal from impurities, generating slag typically at temperatures around 1200 °C. Smelting may involve reduction smelting using carbon-based reductants or matte smelting of sulphide ores, followed by converting and refining to purify the metal. Although the specific processes may vary, most NFS are generated through similar pyrometallurgical routes unless otherwise specified in Table  1 . In addition, certain ores such as lead-zinc and copper-nickel commonly occur together, resulting in mixed slag by-products 19 , 20 . Despite the presence of various industrial terms such as imperial smelting furnace slag, ferronickel slag, copper converter slag, these materials are collectively referred to in this review as LDS, ZS, NS, and CS for clarity. The quantity of slag generated varies significantly depending on the ore grade and extraction process. Non-ferrous metal production can generate 2–16 tonnes of slag per tonne of metal. Accurate global production data for NCS remain limited due to inconsistent reporting and the lack of standardised classification systems. Nevertheless, available literature suggests that global NCS production exceeds 100 Mt annually, with CS representing the largest share, followed by LDS and ZS (see Fig.  3 ). The disposal of certain slags, particularly lead-zinc slags, remains a major environmental concern, with significant quantities reported in landfills in India 21 , the UK 22 , China 23 , and Iran 24 . However, reliable global production data for LTS, NS, and PS are still limited. Regional reports indicate that China dominates LTS and NS production, with approximately 1.2 Mt and 4 Mt produced in 2021 and 2018, respectively, while PS production in 2022 reached 0.8 Mt in India, 3 Mt in the United States, and 8 Mt in China. sections.heading: Physical, chemical, and mineralogical properties
paragraphs: The cooling method and cooling rate of slag significantly influence slag properties and affecting its potential applications like cement or aggregate replacement. Different cooling methods include slow air cooling (air-cooled), controlled water cooling (expanded or foamed), rapid air cooling (pelletized), and high-pressure water cooling (granulated). Air-cooled slag is dense in nature and suitable for use as aggregate. Pelletized and expanded slag are used as lightweight aggregates due to their low density. Granulated slag often exhibits cementitious properties, making it suitable for SCM 26 , 27 . These properties can directly impact the concrete performance, strength, and durability. Physical properties of NCS aggregate from over 22 studies are summarised in Table  2 , while Fig.  4  illustrates their appearance and morphology. LTS and PS aggregate data are relatively scarce, thus highlighting their suitability and higher utilisation for cement replacement in construction materials. Desirable properties like low water absorption, low crushing and impact values, and low LA abrasion values indicate stronger, more durable aggregates with fewer pores 26 , 28 . However, specific requirements may vary based on concrete use and local construction standards. Chemical and mineralogical properties of slag are often bonded together and are crucial for understanding its nature and reaction when used as construction materials. This involves examining major, minor, trace elements, loss on ignition, carbon and sulphur components and stable isotopes. Studies typically use X-ray fluorescence, inductively coupled plasma-mass spectroscopy, inductively coupled plasma-atomic absorption spectroscopy, and mineral analysis with X-ray diffraction (XRD) for chemical and mineral analysis 29 . However, characterising slag’s composition is challenging due to its diverse generation processes and variation in sample preparation for laboratory tests, leading to varying chemical and mineral compositions reported by researchers. Table  4  summarises the mineral composition of NCS based on 22 studies using the Rietveld refinement method to analyse slag’s mineral components, addressing the challenges posed by numerous overlapping peaks in XRD 36 . In addition, amorphous content has been incorporated where available to better reflect the reactive fraction of these materials, as it is well established that the degree of crystallinity significantly influences reactivity. Silicates in NFS, particularly CS, often contain Fe-rich minerals like fayalite, kirschsteinite and hedenbergite. Silicates like quartz, pseudowollastonite, and belite are common in LDS, LTS and PS due to the composition of lead sulphide ore, spodumene ore and phosphate ore being Si-rich, respectively. Furthermore, sulphides, sulphates and oxides containing trace elements like Pb and Zn are found in LDS, LTS and ZS. NS is rich in olivines like forsterite and enstatite due to its Mg-rich nature 27 . These crystalline phases are relatively inert in cementitious systems, which explains the limited reactivity of many NCS when used as SCMs despite favourable oxide compositions. ZS’s mineralogical composition is often analysed without the Rietveld refinement method, with common minerals like quartz, gismondine, fayalite, gehlenite, cordierite, and aluminosilicate being reported.

sections.heading: Utilisation of NCS in cement mortar and concrete materials
Copper slag
paragraphs: CS is widely investigated primarily as aggregate replacement in various concrete types, including SCC, HSC, ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC), RC, SFC and PC. Its relatively high density (3160-3970 kg/m 3 ) and hardness (crushing value of 10-20%), attributed to elevated Fe 2 O 3  (51.82 ± 12.99%), generally improve mechanical performance and abrasion resistance 37 , 38 . However, compared to conventional SCMs such as GGBS and SS, CS contains lower CaO (3.22 ± 2.44%) and Al 2 O 3  (3.89 ± 3.60%), with higher SiO 2  (31.49 ± 5.38%), limiting its intrinsic chemical reactivity as a cement replacement material 39 , 40 . This fundamental compositional difference explains the consistently reported observation that CS performs more effectively as a physical filler or aggregate rather than as a reactive binder.

At low cement replacement levels (5%), CS exhibited performance comparable to control mixes, particularly at low water-to-binder (w/b) ratios, with some studies reporting increased 28 d compressive strength due to limited pozzolanic interaction with Ca(OH) 2  and improved particle packing 41 . Increasing the replacement level to ~15% has been shown to reduce sulphate expansion by up to 50% while maintaining strength 42 . However, this apparent improvement is not solely due to chemical reactivity but also to micro-filler effects and matrix densification, indicating that the contribution of CS is predominantly physical rather than chemical. This distinction is important in explaining discrepancies across studies that attribute strength gains to “pozzolanic activity” without considering packing effects.

The use of CS as fine aggregate replacement has been more extensively validated although reported optimum replacement levels vary significantly across studies 43 , 44 . Al-Jabri et al. 45  reported that 40% CS achieved the highest 28-day compressive strength, while 60% replacement yielded strength comparable to control mixes. Beyond this range (80-100%), strength reductions are consistently observed due to increased free water content arising from the low water absorption of CS, which improves workability but weakens the matrix. Microstructural analysis revealed improved bonding in the 40% CS mix 46 , whereas excessive CS content leads to increased voids and weaker microstructure 47 , potentially exacerbated by impurities in CS 48 . These findings highlight that conflicting results in the literature are largely governed by differences in replacement level, water content, and particle characteristics rather than inconsistencies in material behaviour.

Interestingly, structural performance does not always follow the same trend as compressive strength. Prem et al. 49  reported improved flexure response in RC beams with 100% CS fine aggregate, indicating improved load-carrying capacity despite potential reduction in compressive strength. Similarly, hybrid systems combining CS with other materials show mixed outcomes. While partial replacement of cement with GGBS in CS- containing mixes may reduce strength, an optimised combination (30% GGBS and 50% CS) produced the highest strength enhancement 50 , indicating a strong synergy between binder reactivity and aggregate packing. The incorporation of fibres, such as polypropylene fibre, further improves crack control and supports strength development 51 , reinforcing the importance of multi-material optimisation.

In SCC systems, CS plays a dual role by enhancing both workability and strength within an optimal range. The incorporation of 30% CS significantly improves compressive strength at all curing ages; however, exceeding 60% leads to the formation of voids, pores, and microcracks, as shown in Fig.  6 52 . This again reflects the trade-off between improved flowability (due to low water absorption) and reduced structural integrity. Sharma and Khan 53  further demonstrated that replacing silica fume (SF) with fly ash (FA) in CS-based systems reduces filling ability, although high CS content (60%) improves flowability. The addition of 10% SF enhances compressive strength through micro-filler effects and densification of the interfacial transition zone. In ternary blends, however, replacing 10% metakaolin (MK) with FA results in strength reduction even at full CS replacement, despite improved compactness 54 . These results highlight that binder composition plays a critical role in governing CS performance, particularly in highly flowable systems. Fig. 6 Microstructural evolution of SCC incorporating CS at different replacement levels. SEM images show the influence of increasing CS replacement on the microstructure of SCC at 28 d.  a  Control mix (0% CS) exhibiting micro-cracks, voids, and the presence of ettringite.  b  20% CS replacement showing the formation of denser calcium–silicate–hydrate (C–S–H) layers with reduced porosity.  c  30% CS replacement characterised by the accumulation of dense calcium silicate hydrate (CSH) phases, contributing to a more compact microstructure.  d  40% CS replacement displaying a refined matrix with ettringite formation and reduced voids.  e  60% CS replacement showing increased porosity and a higher number of voids, indicating reduced microstructural integrity at higher replacement levels. Source: adapted from Ref.  234  with permission.

For the HSC application, similar trends are observed. Al-Jabri et al. 55  reported increased density and improved workability with increasing CS content, with up to 50% replacement yielding comparable strength to the control mixes. However, beyond 80%, compressive strength declines due to excess free water and increased porosity. The reduced water demand (up to ~22% at 100% CS replacement) further confirms the role of CS in modifying rheology rather than contributing to hydration 56 . Wu et al. 57  identified an optimum replacement level of ~40%, achieving a 20% improvement in dynamic compression, with performance declining at higher levels due to microstructural defects. The incorporating steel fibre and nano-materials significantly alters this behaviour. Steel fibre reinforcement enhances compressive and tensile performance, particularly at high CS contents 58 ,  59 – 60 , while nano-silica addition (1%) reduces voids and capillary porosity, leading to improved overall strength 61 . In UHPC systems, optimised particle packing and curing conditions are critical. Ambily et al. 62  demonstrated that a binary grading system (70% coarse and 30% fine CS fractions) maximises packing density, achieving compressive strength exceeding 150 MPa under heat curing. Similarly, ground CS combined with heat curing can achieve strengths up to 235 MPa 60 , highlighting the importance of particle refinement and curing regime in overcoming the limitations of CS.

Although less extensively studied, the utilisation of CS as coarse aggregate also shows promising performance. Sharifi et al. 63  reported that full replacement of natural coarse aggregate with CS resulted in higher early strength, with compressive strength increasing by 8-27% over 28 d when mix design (particularly w/b ratio) is optimised. Khanzadi and Behnood 64  similarly found that 100% CS aggregate outperformed limestone aggregate due to improved mechanical interlocking. In pervious concrete, Lori et al. 37  identified 60% CS as the optimal replacement level, achieving improved mechanical properties while maintaining porosity comparable to conventional aggregates.

A key development in recent studies is the distinction between primary and secondary CS. Secondary CS exhibits reduced Fe 2 O 3  (49.10 ± 3.12%) and increased CaO (5.20 ± 1.90%), SiO 2  (26.57 ± 2.47%) and Al 2 O 3  (4.33 ± 1.40%), resulting in improved reactivity compared to primary CS. Edwin et al. 65  demonstrated that 5% secondary CS enhances binder reactions in ultra-high performance mortar, while up to 20% replacement yields compressive strength comparable to or exceeding control mixes at early ages. However, further studies by Edwin et al. 66 , 67  showed that processing conditions, such as vacuum mixing and heat treatment, have a more significant influence on performance than the presence of secondary CS itself. Notably, normal curing conditions without heat treatment were sufficient to stabilise potentially harmful elements, enabling safe utilisation of secondary CS at up to 50% as an aggregate and 20% as cement replacement.

sections.heading: Nickel slag
paragraphs: NS is primarily utilised in cement and concrete as a fine aggregate replacement due to its favourable physical properties, including low water absorption (0.60-1.70%), low crushing value (3.50–4.60%), and Los Angeles abrasion value (13.30–22.00%), similar to CS. NS typically contains 45.33 ± 9.32% SiO 2 , 24.72 ± 8.30% MgO and 28.66 ± 18.89% FeO, with relatively low CaO (7.22 ± 10.47%) and Al 2 O 3  (6.68 ± 5.20%) contents 27 . This composition limits its hydraulic reactivity, as the low CaO and Al 2 O 3  contents restrict the formation of conventional cement hydration products such as CSH and calcium aluminate phases.

A major concern associated with NS is its high MgO content (>20%), which is generally linked to volumetric instability due to the formation of expansive Mg(OH) 2  during hydration. However, a critical examination of the literature indicates that this risk is often overestimated. Several studies have shown that MgO in NS predominantly exists in stable crystalline phases, such as forsterite or magnesioferrite, rather than as free MgO, significantly reducing its reactivity. This explains the apparent contradiction between theoretical expansion risk and experimental observation. For example, Rahman et al. 68  reported slightly lower strength in NS-blended mortar due to reduced CaO availability, yet soundness remained within acceptable limits.

Similarly, Zhai et al. 69  found no detectable Mg(OH) 2  formation even in NS with relatively high MgO content, attributing this to the stability of Mg-bearing phases. From a reactivity perspective, NS exhibits limited early-age activity but demonstrates some pozzolanic contribution at later age. Microstructural analysis revealed the CSH gel and stable ferroan forsterite phases, with amorphous SiO 2  participating in secondary reactions. Consequently, 20% NS achieved 93% and 67% of the control compressive strength at 90 d, indicating poor later strength development. This behaviour is consistent with the findings in Han et al. 70  and explains why Bouasria et al. 71  identified a lower optimum cement replacement level (~10%) for maintaining mechanical performance. These variations in optimum replacement levels highlight that NS performance is strongly governed by its limited reactivity and dilution effects at higher replacement ratios.

In NS-blended concrete, the influence of NS on hydration products and microstructure is more complex. Huang et al. 72  reported that 30% NS replacement reduces the Ca/Si ratio in CSH gel and improved silicate chain polymerisation, resulting in lower compressive strength but improved chloride resistance. This apparent trade-off between strength and durability is a recurring trend in NS systems. Further studies by Liu et al. 73  confirmed that NS contributes to pore refinement and densification over time due to continued hydration and CSH formation. Kim et al. 74  identified the formation of hydrotalcite-like phases in NS-blended concrete, which is uncommon in conventional cement systems and suggests secondary hydration involving Mg-bearing phases. Chen et al. 75  attributed improved chloride binding capacity to the combined effects of hydrotalcite formation and CSH gel development. These findings indicate that, although NS has limited direct reactivity, it can enhance durability through microstructural modification and secondary phase formation.

When used as a fine aggregate, NS demonstrates more consistent and beneficial performance. Compressive strength improves with NS replacement up to an optimum level, typically 50%, achieving up to 84 MPa at a w/c of 0.3 76 . This improvement is primarily attributed to enhanced particle packing and increased density rather than chemical reactivity. Beyond this level, strength decreases due to increased void content and the coarser particle size of NS, which weakens the matrix 77 . However, Chen et al. 78  reported a slightly higher optimum replacement level (~60%) when using a well-graded NS-sand mixture (0.60–2.36 mm), demonstrating that gradation plays a critical role in performance. These differences explain the variation in reported optimum values across studies and emphasise the importance of aggregate grading in NS utilisation. Figure  7  shows the optimum NS aggregate replacement level for both graded and ungraded mixed sand. Similar trends are observed in concrete, where NS improves density and interfacial bonding 79 . Edwin et al. 80  attributed strength enhancement to improved cohesion and slip resistance due to the angular shape of NS particles. Ngii et al. 81  further suggested that a limited pozzolanic interaction between SiO 2  in NS and Ca(OH) 2  contributes to interface strengthening. However, this contribution is secondary compared to physical effects. Liu et al. 82  confirmed that NS radioactivity remains within acceptable limits according to Chinese standard, although the need for pre-assessment is highlighted, particularly for high MgO slags 83 . Fig. 7 Mechanical properties of NS mortar and concrete at varying replacement levels. a  Compressive strength development of mortar incorporating NS at different replacement levels (0–100%) measured at 7 days, 28 days and 56 days. The results indicate that a 50% replacement level provides the optimum compressive strength compared to other mixtures.  b  Compressive strength and  c  flexural strength of concrete prepared with graded mixed sand incorporating NS at different replacement levels (0–100%) evaluated at 3 days, 14 days and 28 days. Both strength properties show improved performance up to 60% replacement, beyond which a reduction is observed. The highlighted regions indicate the optimum replacement levels for mechanical performance. Source: (a) adapted from Ref.  77 .; (b) and (c) adapted from Ref.  78 . with permission.

The performance of NS can be further enhanced in blended systems. Nguyen Quang et al. 84  demonstrated that replacing sand with NS in FA-blended concrete significantly improves strength compared to FA-only systems, indicating that NS can offset the slow early-age reactivity of FA. This aligns with the observation by Saha and Sarker 85 , where FA delays early strength but contributes to later-age performance through pozzolanic reactions. Similarly, Nuruzzaman et al. 86  reported that incorporating FA and GGBS in NS-based SCC reduces porosity and chloride penetration while increasing compressive strength (from 50 MPa to 66 MPa at 40% NS). These results highlight the importance of synergistic interactions in improving NS performance.

In terms of durability under extreme conditions, Sun et al. 87  showed that a combination of 75% GGBS and 25% NS enhances fire resistance without compromising workability and mechanical properties, demonstrating the suitability of NS in high-performance applications when combined with other materials. As shown in Fig.  8 , Gu et al. 88  reported significant improvements in both compressive (37.2%) and flexural (26.5%) strengths in limestone calcined clay cement (LC3) blended concrete with 100% NS aggregate compared to standard sand. This indicates that advanced binder systems, such as LC3, can effectively compensate for the low reactivity of NS and enable higher replacement levels. Fig. 8 Mechanical performance of LC3 blended concrete incorporating NS at varying replacement levels and w/b ratios. a  Compressive strength and  b  flexural strength of concrete mixtures incorporating NS at different replacement levels and w/b ratios of 0.5 and 0.45. The mix notation is defined as follows: C1 represents normal concrete with w/b = 0.5, and C2 represents normal concrete with w/b = 0.45. L denotes LC3 concrete. N refers to NS, and the number following N indicates the replacement level (10%, 20%, and 30%). The results show variations in strength with increasing NS content, with optimal performance observed at specific replacement levels depending on the mix type and w/b ratio. Source: adapted from Ref.  88 . with permission.

sections.heading: Lead slag and zinc slag (lead-zinc slag)
paragraphs: LDS and ZS are often discussed together as by-products of lead-zinc smelting processes, although variations in smelting routes and cooling conditions result in notable differences in their properties. Both slags are primarily composed of Fe 2 O 3 , SiO 2 , and Al 2 O 3 , with minor amounts of CaO, MgO, PbO, and ZnO. The presence of PbO and ZnO is a key distinguishing feature compared to other NCS and represents a major challenge for their utilisation in cementitious systems. Dissolved Pb 2+  and Zn 2+  ions can retard cement hydration by forming gelatinous layers or hydroxide precipitates around cement grains, thereby inhibiting the nucleation and growth of hydration products. This mechanism explains many of the inconsistencies reported in the literature regarding strength development and setting behaviour.

From a reactivity standpoint, LDS and ZS contain sufficient SiO 2  and Al 2 O 3  to potentially exhibit pozzolanic behaviour; however, their effectiveness as SCMs is highly condition-dependent. For instance, mortar containing 30% lead-zinc tailings shows insufficient compressive strength 89 , indicating that dilution effects and low intrinsic reactivity dominate at high replacement levels. In contrast, Zhao et al. 90  reported that reducing particle size to 8.30 μm significantly enhances compressive strength across all ages, highlighting that particle refinement is a critical factor governing reactivity. Similarly, Penpolcharoen 91  observed that secondary LDS exhibits magnetic properties associated with its CaO–FeO–SiO 2  structures, contributing primarily through a filler and densification effects rather than true pozzolanic reactions.

Recent findings provide further insight into this apparent contradiction. Yang et al. 92  reported that lead-zinc slag contains a high amorphous content (~96%), primarily composed of (alumino)silicate and Fe-rich phases. R³ testing confirms that it exhibits significant pozzolanic reactivity, albeit lower than GGBS. This reduced reactivity is mainly attributed to its relatively coarse particle size and highly polymerised, low-calcium silicate network. Despite this, blended systems incorporating 10–30% lead-zinc slag achieved compressive strengths comparable to OPC at later ages. Furthermore, leaching tests confirmed minimal heavy metal release below regulatory limits, while environmental assessments demonstrated a reduction in global warming potential, supporting its feasibility as a sustainable SCM. These results suggest that discrepancies in reported performance are primarily due to differences in particle size, amorphous content, and mix design rather than fundamental limitations of the material.

Recent studies highlight the effective valorisation of lead-zinc slags in advanced cementitious systems. For instance, Yang et al. 93  showed that combining lead-zinc tailings as filler with lead-zinc slag as a SCM enables UHPC with high performance, low porosity, and complete heavy-metal immobilisation, even at high replacement levels. Similarly, Gu et al. 94  demonstrated that the reactivity of lead-zinc slag can be enhanced by co-utilisation with 5% magnesium-rich lime mud, at the same time reducing global warming potential by up to 43% compared to that of OPC mixtures. These findings highlight that multi-component approaches are essential to unlock the full potential of LDS and ZS.

In terms of aggregate applications, the relatively high specific gravity of LDS and ZS (2.21–3.88) compared to natural aggregates is attributed to their elevated FeO/Fe 2 O 3  content, making them suitable as heavy aggregates. Alwaeli 95  reported that concrete incorporating 100% LDS as fine aggregate exhibited higher compressive strength and improved gamma radiation shielding compared to conventional concrete. Similarly, Saca et al. 96  showed that partial replacement of coarse aggregates with LDS enhances radiation shielding performance. The strength improvement is primarily attributed to increased density and improved interfacial bonding 97 , while Saikia et al. 98  observed improved workability and reduced air content at up to 35% LDS replacement. These consistent findings indicate that LDS performs reliably as an aggregate due to its physical properties, regardless of its limited chemical reactivity.

In contrast, ZS exhibits more variable performance, particularly when used in cementitious systems. Despite its high density (3600–3900 kg/m 3 ), increasing ZS content often leads to reduced compressive strength 99 . This counterintuitive behaviour is attributed to the hydrophobic properties and glassy surface of ZS, which affects water distribution and reduces effective bonding between cement paste and aggregate. Additionally, Morrison et al. 22  highlighted that Pb and Zn ions can delay hydration through the formation of gelatinous layers, further contributing to strength reduction. However, the inclusion of FA and GGBS can mitigate this effect by modifying the hydration environment and reducing susceptibility to alkali-silica reaction. Nevertheless, the lower CaO content in such blended systems may lead to reduced strength 100 , demonstrating a trade-off between durability improvement and mechanical performance.

On the contrary, some studies report minimal negative effects of heavy metals on hydration. Saikia et al. 101  reported that LDS does not interfere with hydration rate and exhibits comparable compressive strength compared to natural fine aggregates. This discrepancy suggests that the influence of PbO and ZnO is not solely dependent on their presence but also on their chemical state, solubility, and interaction with the cement matrix. Further mitigation strategies include the use of additives. For example, the addition of marble dust improves workability and reduces demoulding difficulty in ZS-containing mixes, likely due to the presence of Ca 2+  ions from dolomite, which counteract hydration retardation 102 . This is consistent with findings by Weeks et al. 103 , who showed that Group II elements-based additives are more effective than Group I in overcoming ZS-induced retardation. As shown in Fig.  9 , chlorides and nitrates of Group II elements significantly enhance hydration kinetics, producing heat evolution profiles comparable to control mixes. Fig. 9 Influence of additive type and concentration on hydration kinetics of ZS mortar. a  Effect of high concentrations and  b  low concentrations of various chemical additives on the maximum rate of heat output and hydration onset time of ZS mortar. The plots present the relationship between heat evolution and the time to onset of hydration for different additives. Data points represent different chemical activators, including chlorides, nitrates, and hydroxides, while the sand control is shown for comparison. A vertical dashed line at 16 hours indicates the threshold separating accelerated and delayed hydration behaviour. Variations in additive type and concentration significantly influence both the rate and timing of hydration, with certain additives promoting early hydration and higher heat release, while others retard the reaction. Source: adapted from Ref.  103 . with permission.

A direct comparison between LDS and ZS further highlights their distinct behaviours. Mosavinezhad and Nabavi 104  reported that concrete with 30% ZS exhibited an 88% strength reduction compared to the control mixes, whereas LDS at the same replacement level maintained comparable strength. This stark contrast highlights the influence of physical properties and chemical interactions on performance. Tripathi et al. 21  suggested that 60% ZS is the upper limit for maintaining acceptable strength, with slight improvements at early ages under low w/c conditions. Field applications, however, demonstrate that ZS can still be viable under practical conditions, as a ZS concrete roadway achieved 28 d strength of 40 MPa and showed no deterioration after one year of service 105 .

sections.heading: Phosphorus slag
paragraphs: PS is solely used for cement replacement rather than aggregate replacement due to its relatively lower density (1220–1290 kg/m 3 ), irregular shapes and larger particle size compared to conventional aggregates. To date, there is no reported application of PS as an aggregate replacement in cement mortar and concrete, which contrasts with other NCS, such as CS and NS, that are widely used in aggregate form. This limitation highlights that the primary value of PS lies in its potential as an SCM rather than a structural filler.

Chemically, PS contains a significant amount of CaO (44.80 ± 4.86%) and SiO 2  (38.47 ± 3.17%), with moderate Al 2 O 3  (4.49 ± 1.75%), giving it a composition broadly comparable to GGBS. However, despite this similarity, PS consistently exhibits lower reactivity than GGBS, primarily due to its lower Al 2 O 3  content and differences in glass structure 106 , 107 . The presence of amorphous SiO 2  and Al 2 O 3  enables PS to participate in pozzolanic reactions with Ca(OH) 2 , forming additional CSH gel and contributing to matrix densification 108 , 109 . This explains why several studies report improved long-term mechanical performance in PS-blended systems. For instance, Wang et al. 110  and Lv et al. 111  observed that concrete containing 20-35% PS exhibited up to 33% higher compressive strength growth rates compared to FA-blended concrete at 7 d and beyond, indicating that PS may outperform FA in later-age strength development.

However, a critical limitation of PS is the presence of P 2 O 5  (2.64 ± 0.92%), which introduces a distinct retardation mechanism not observed in other slags 112 . Phosphate ions react with Ca 2+  ions to form hydroxyapatite (Ca 10 (PO 4 ) 6 (OH) 2 ), reducing the availability of Ca 2+  in the pore solution and hindering the nucleation and growth of hydration products. In addition, the formation of phosphoric acid lowers the pH of the system, further suppressing early hydration 113 . This explains the commonly reported observation of delayed setting and reduced early strength in PS-blended systems, despite its favourable long-term performance. Therefore, the contradictory behaviour of PS (low early strength but improved later strength) is primarily governed by the interaction between its phosphate content and cement hydration kinetics.

To overcome these limitations, various activation strategies have been explored. Mechanical activation is the most widely adopted approach due to its direct influence on particle size and reactivity. Increasing fineness enhances the specific surface area and dissolution rate of PS, accelerating the release of reactive silica and calcium, and partially offsetting the phosphate-induced retardation. Pang and An 114  and Wang et al. 115  reported that increasing the Blaine fineness significantly improves compressive strength and microstructure at 20-40% replacement levels. Similarly, Wang et al. 116  found that finely ground PS exhibits higher strength than finely ground FA, suggesting comparatively higher latent reactivity under optimised conditions. However, this improvement is not linear. Beyond a certain fineness threshold, strength gains diminish or even decline due to particle agglomeration and excessive water demand 117 , 118 . He et al. 30  demonstrated that a d50 of 6.07 μm yields optimal performance, while further reduction to 2.02 μm results in decreased strength. This highlights a key trade-off between reactivity and workability in mechanically activated PS systems.

Wet grinding has been shown to be particularly effective in enhancing PS performance. Su et al. 119  reported that wet-ground PS significantly improves both setting behaviour and compressive strength compared to untreated PS, as shown in Fig.  10 . Similarly, Jinhui et al. 120  demonstrated that optimising cement fineness (520 m 2 /kg) in combination with PS is more effective than excessive grinding PS alone. Huang et al. 121  further showed that wet milling for 120 minutes provides an optimal balance between performance and energy consumption, achieving 36% higher 28 d strength at 40% PS replacement compared to OPC systems. Fig. 10 Effect of particle size on setting time and compressive strength of cement mortar incorporating PS. a  Initial and final setting times and  b  compressive strength of cement mortar incorporating 30% wet-ground PS with varying particle sizes (25 μm, 9 μm, 4 μm, and 2 μm). The bar charts show that decreasing particle size leads to reduced setting time and enhanced compressive strength. Dashed horizontal lines represent control values for comparison, while highlighted regions indicate mixtures with the most significant performance improvements. Compressive strength is evaluated at 3 days, 7 days and 28 days, demonstrating progressive strength development with finer PS particles. Source: adapted from Ref 119 . with permission.

Thermal activation provides another pathway to enhance PS reactivity but involves higher energy consumption. Steam curing, commonly used in precast applications, accelerates hydration and compensates for early strength loss. Peng et al. 122  reported that steam curing at 95 °C for 3 d produced compressive strength up to 156 MPa in HSC containing 35% PS, primarily due to accelerated consumption of Ca(OH) 2  and enhanced CSH formation. Similar trends have been reported in vast literature 123 ,  124 – 125 . Alternatively, Liu et al. 126  explored calcination of PS prior to use. As shown in Fig.  11 , increasing calcination temperature transforms PS from an amorphous to a more crystalline state, with optimal performance observed at ~800 °C, where early strength increased by 55%. However, further increases in temperature reduce long-term strength due to the formation of stable crystalline phases that hinder the dissolution of silica and alumina. This demonstrates a fundamental trade-off between short-term activation and long-term reactivity. Fig. 11 Influence of calcination temperature on phase composition and compressive strength of PS. a  XRD patterns of uncalcined and calcined PS at different temperatures (100–1000 °C), showing the evolution of crystalline phases. Major identified phases include wollastonite (CaSiO 3 ), cuspidine (Ca 4 Si 2 O 7 F 2 ), and fluorapatite (Ca 5 (PO 4 ) 3 F), with increasing peak intensity indicating enhanced crystallinity at higher calcination temperatures.  b  Compressive strength of cement mortar incorporating calcined PS, measured at 3 days, 7 days and 28 days. The results demonstrate that calcination temperature significantly affects strength development, with optimal performance observed at intermediate temperatures, followed by a reduction at higher temperatures. Source: adapted from Ref.  126 . with permission.

Compared to mechanical and thermal methods, chemical activation offers a more energy-efficient approach by directly modifying the hydration environment. Pang et al. 127  reported that chemical additives promote ettringite formation, enhancing early strength development. Similarly, Allahverdi and Mahinroosta 128  and Yong et al. 129  demonstrated that sodium sulphate increases system alkalinity, counteracting the acidifying effect of P 2 O 5  and improving hydration kinetics. The use of supplementary materials also plays a critical role. Su and Li 130  and Li and Zhang 131  showed that red mud can synergistically enhance PS reactivity, contributing to the formation of both CSH gel and calcium aluminate hydrate. Lin et al. 132  further demonstrated that combining PS with FA leads to improved early strength compared to single-material systems, with SEM analysis (Fig.  12 ) confirming additional CSH gel formation on FA particle surfaces. Fig. 12 Microstructural characteristics of mortar incorporating phosphorus slag PS and FA at different replacement levels. SEM images showing the microstructure of mortar at 28 d with varying proportions of PS and FA.  a  30% PS exhibiting relatively dense matrix regions with some plate-like particles and limited porosity.  b  40% PS showing increased microcracking and voids, indicating a less compact structure at higher replacement levels.  c  15% PS + 15% FA demonstrating the presence of spherical FA particles embedded within the matrix, contributing to improved packing density.  d  30% PS + 20% FA showing a heterogeneous microstructure with a combination of unreacted particles, voids, and fibrous hydration products. These observations highlight the influence of combined PS and FA replacement on microstructural development and matrix densification. Source: adapted from Ref.  132 . with permission.

More recently, PS has also been incorporated into low-clinker and clinker-free systems where its contribution becomes more significant due to synergistic reactions with other binders 133 ,  134 – 135 . Yang et al. 136  reported enhanced UHPC performance in PS-FA systems with the addition of SF and polycarboxylic-ether, achieving higher 28 d strength than control mixes. This highlights that PS is most effective when used a part of a multi-component system rather than as a standalone replacement, reinforcing the importance of mix design optimisation. The improved long-term strength development in such systems is attributed to sustained pozzolanic reaction and microstructural refinement 137 .

sections.heading: Lithium slag
paragraphs: Similar to PS, LTS is solely used for cement replacement rather than aggregate replacement, largely due to its fine particle characteristics and lack of suitability as a structural filler. Chemically, LTS is dominated by amorphous SiO 2  (>50%), with additional Al 2 O 3  (21.39 ± 2.51%) and CaO (7.02 ± 3.73%), making its composition broadly comparable to FA. This similarity suggests that LTS can function as an SCM without requiring intensive pre-treatment such as calcination. However, unlike highly reactive SCMs such as GGBS, the performance of LTS is strongly governed by its relatively low intrinsic reactivity and dependence on external calcium sources 138 . Rahman et al. 139  reported that LTS contains 31.6% amorphous phase, which participates in pozzolanic reactions during cement hydration. Nevertheless, this amorphous content is lower than that of highly reactive slags, limiting its early reactivity. As a result, contradictory performance trends are commonly reported in the literature. For example, He et al. 140  observed that increasing LTS replacement leads to a reduction in early strength, whereas moderate replacement levels (10–20%) improve later-age performance. Specifically, 20% LTS achieved the highest 90-day compressive strength, indicating that LTS contributes primarily to long-term strength development rather than early hydration.

This behaviour is consistent with the fundamental reaction mechanism of LTS. Its pozzolanic activity depends heavily on the availability of Ca(OH)2 from cement hydration 141 . Consequently, Qin et al. 142  reported that beyond 20% replacement, LTS increasingly behaves as an inert filler in RCAC, with unreacted particles increasing porosity and reducing compressive strength. This explains the apparent contradiction where LTS enhances strength at moderate levels but deteriorates performance at higher dosages.

Despite these limitations, LTS provides notable durability benefits. For instance, 10% LTS replacement significantly reduces chloride ion permeability, particularly in C30 concrete, indicating a good balance between strength and durability 143 . In addition, LTS demonstrates superior resistance to acid attack. Zhang et al. 144  reported that concrete with 40% LTS subjected to 100 days of simulated acid rain exposure exhibited higher compressive strength than the control group, as shown in Fig.  13 . This improved performance is attributed to the formation of a denser microstructure and reduced permeability, highlighting that LTS may be more beneficial in durability-driven applications rather than strength. Fig. 13 Surface degradation and compressive strength evolution of concrete incorporating LTS under simulated acid rain exposure. a  Visual appearance of concrete containing 20% LTS after exposure to simulated acid rain at different corrosion ages (20 d, 60 d, 80 d, and 100 d). Progressive surface deterioration is observed with increasing exposure time, including discoloration, roughening, and aggregate exposure, indicating material degradation.  b  Compressive strength of concrete mixtures with varying LTS contents (0%, 20%, and 40%) as a function of corrosion age. The curves show strength reduction over time, with distinct early-stage and middle-to-late-stage degradation behaviour. Mixtures with LTS exhibit comparatively improved resistance to strength loss under prolonged acid exposure, with higher LTS content showing better retention of compressive strength. Source: adapted from Ref.  144 . with permission.

The slow reactivity of LTS is further influenced by its interaction with hydration products. Although gypsum present in LTS can promote early ettringite formation 145 , studies by Qi et al. 146  and Zhou et al. 147  indicate that the overall ettringite content may decrease due to the consumption of Ca(OH) 2  by pozzolanic reactions. This highlights a competitive reaction mechanism, where LTS simultaneously contributes to and limits hydration processes, depending on system composition. Such competing mechanisms explain the variability in reported results across different studies.

To address these limitations, synergistic blending with other SCMs has been widely investigated. Luo et al. 148  and Gu et al. 149  demonstrated that combining LTS with GGBS or SS enhances reactivity by supplying additional Ca(OH) 2  and improving the overall hydration environment. For example, mixtures containing 75% cement, 20% LTS, and 5% GGBS achieved the highest compressive strength, while 70% cement, 20% LTS, and 10% SS also showed significant improvement. This indicates that LTS performs more effectively in blended systems rather than as a standalone SCM, consistent with observations for other low-reactivity slags.

In the HSC application, LTS shows promising behaviour when used in combination with other supplementary materials. Wu et al. 150  reported that 10% LTS yields peak compressive strength at 28 d in HSC. Furthermore, binary systems incorporating both FA and LTS (each at 10%) achieved superior later strength due to synergistic pozzolanic reactions. In UHPC, He et al. 151  and Li and Huang 152  identified 10% LTS as the optimum replacement level for SF, achieving 28 d compressive strength of 145 MPa and 112 MPa, respectively. These improvements are attributed to the combined effects of particle packing, filler action, and secondary hydration, resulting in a denser microstructure, as shown in Fig.  14 . Zhang et al. 153  further demonstrated that combining LTS with limestone powder enhances UHPC performance, with an optimal LTS:LP ratio of 2:1 at a total replacement of 30%. Although LTS does not inherently require activation, additional treatments can further enhance its performance. Calcination at ~600 °C has been shown to improve early strength and hydration kinetics while maintaining long-term performance and significantly enhancing flexural strength in UHPC systems 154 , 155 . However, this introduces additional energy demand, raising consideration regarding the overall sustainability of such approaches. Fig. 14 Microstructural characteristics of UHPC incorporating LTS and SF at different replacement levels. SEM images showing the microstructure of UHPC at 28 d with varying proportions of SF and LTS.  a  20% SF exhibiting a relatively dense matrix with compact hydration products.  b  15% SF + 5% LTS showing a slightly heterogeneous structure with moderate densification.  c  10% SF + 10% LTS characterised by the presence of abundant needle-like crystalline phases, indicating increased formation of ettringite or similar hydration products.  d  5% SF + 15% LTS displaying a less dense matrix with visible pores and reduced compactness at higher LTS content. Source: adapted from Ref.  151 . with permission.

sections.heading: Critical discussion on challenges, future prospect, and research directions
paragraphs: Over the past two decades, increasing attention has been directed toward NCS, including CS, LDS, LTS, NS, PS, and ZS, for their potential utilisation in cement mortar and various types of concrete. Unlike conventional SCMs such as GGBS, these materials exhibit highly variable chemical compositions, mineralogy, and physical properties, which fundamentally govern their performance in cementitious systems. This variability is the primary reason why NCS remain under-utilised despite their demonstrated potential.

A key distinction among NCS lies in their functional role. Materials such as CS, NS, and LDS are predominantly effective as aggregate replacements, where performance is governed mainly by physical properties such as density, hardness, and particle morphology. In contrast, PS and LTS are primarily utilised as cement replacements, where chemical reactivity and hydration mechanisms become dominant. ZS is largely limited to aggregate applications due to its hydration-retarding behaviour.

In this review, the optimal replacement level mainly refers to the replacement range associated with the best compressive strength performance reported in the literature, as compressive strength remains the most commonly used indicator for evaluating the practical utilisation of NCS in cementitious systems. Based on this perspective, the reported replacement ranges from the literature are summarised in Fig.  15 . Table  5  summarises the critical comparison of NCS as cement replacement materials. Despite the promising potential of NCS in cement-based materials, several challenges remain before their large-scale adoption in the construction industry can be fully realised. One major challenge lies in the variability of NCS properties, which largely depend on ore sources, smelting conditions, and cooling processes. Such variability influences the chemical composition, mineralogical phases, and reactivity of slags, leading to inconsistent performance in cement and concrete systems. Future research should therefore prioritise the development of standardised characterisation methods to enable more reliable evaluation and utilisation of different NCS types. Another important aspect concerns the activation and processing technologies required to improve the reactivity of NCS. Many slags exhibit lower intrinsic reactivity compared with conventional SCMs and may require pre-treatment processes such as mechanical grinding, chemical activation, or thermal treatment. Emerging activation strategies, including nano-modification 156 , 157 , alkali activation 158 , 159 , and carbonation treatment 160 , 161  of NCS, may offer promising pathways to improve the cementitious performance of NCS, engineering performance, and environmental benefits.

Recent studies demonstrate that nano-modification can effectively improve the reactivity of low-reactivity or highly crystalline slags 162 . For example, nano-SiO 2  appears particularly suitable for Ca-rich and weakly reactive slags such as SS because it accelerates hydration and promotes additional CSH formation. Zhou et al. 163  reported that nano-SiO 2  on SS surfaces significantly enhanced hydration activity and reduced porosity. In contrast, carbon-based nanomaterials such as graphene are more compatible with highly siliceous slags such as LTS, where the nanomaterial primarily improves dispersion, nucleation, and interfacial bonding. Zhang et al. 164  showed that nano-graphene-coated LTS improved secondary hydration and increased compressive and flexural strengths. Similarly, nano-TiO 2  may be more suitable for slags with slower hydration kinetics, such as NS and PS, due to its strong nucleation effect and ability to accelerate early-age hydration 165 . The compatibility between nanomaterials and NCS largely depends on slag chemistry, amorphous content, and hydration characteristics, suggesting that future studies should focus on tailoring specific nano-modification strategies for different NCS systems rather than adopting a universal approach.

Alkali activation, although it is beyond the main scope of this cement-based review, has emerged as a promising route for valorising NCS. Unlike conventional SCM systems, alkali activation allows the use of high-volume or even 100% slag content without OPC 166 , 167 . Slags with high amorphous SiO 2  and Al 2 O 3  contents, such as PS 168 , LTS 169 , and certain lead-zinc slag 170 , are particularly suitable due to their ability to form aluminosilicate gels under alkaline environments. For instances, Jia et al. 171  highlighted that the workability of alkali-activated PS is highly dependent on alkali dosage and silicate modulus, where balanced pore solution chemistry can stabilise hydration and reduce rapid stiffening. Zhang et al. 172  showed that alkali-activated LTS systems can improve matrix densification and late-age strength through the formation of various hydrate gels, while Chen et al. 173  reported that lead-zinc fine can accelerate binder reactions and enhance early-age strength by increasing pore solution alkalinity.

Carbonation treatment also represents a promising pathway, particularly for Ca-rich slags such as PS. PS is more amenable to mineral carbonation because their reactive calcium-bearing phases can readily form stable carbonate products 174 . He et al. 175  reported that carbonation treatment significantly improved the mechanical performance and microstructure of PS, achieving compressive strength exceeding 120 MPa under optimal carbonation conditions. The carbonation process promoted the formation of carbonate products, reduced porosity by 30%, and enabled CO 2  sequestration of up to 72 kg per ton of PS, highlighting the strong carbonation potential of PS for sustainable construction applications. By contrast, highly siliceous slags such as CS, LDS, NS, LTS, and ZS are less favourable for direct carbonation due to their lower calcium availability. Therefore, future carbonation studies should prioritise Ca-rich NCS systems like PS.

From an environmental perspective, a more quantitative assessment of sustainability impacts is needed. While NCS utilisation can reduce landfill disposal and conserve natural resources, pre-treatment processes such as grinding and activation may require additional energy input. Tamoor et al. 176  highlighted that the environmental and economic sustainability of cementitious materials must be evaluated together through life cycle assessment (LCA), CO 2  emission analysis, and long-term durability considerations. Their study showed that although alternative binders and SCM-based systems can significantly reduce environmental impact, energy-intensive activation processes may offset some sustainability benefits. Therefore, future studies should incorporate LCA, CO 2  emission analysis, and energy balance evaluations to better quantify the environmental benefits and potential trade-offs associated with NCS utilisation 177 .

In addition, although untreated NCS may exhibit relatively high heavy-metal leaching due to the presence of Pb, Zn, Cr, and other trace elements, many previous studies reported that incorporating these slags into cementitious systems can significantly reduce leaching concentrations through physical encapsulation and chemical immobilisation within hydration products and dense concrete matrices 92 , 178 , 179 . Nevertheless, the long-term environmental safety of NCS-containing concrete remains insufficiently understood. Potential risks associated with heavy metal leaching, chemical stability, and exposure under aggressive environmental conditions require more systematic investigation using standardised environmental assessment methods and regulatory frameworks. Given the limited environmental safety data currently available for many NCS types, future research should prioritise comprehensive leaching assessment and long-term durability studies to ensure the safe and reliable large-scale utilisation of NCS in infrastructure applications.

Last but not least, the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning offers promising opportunities to accelerate research on NCS 180 , 181 . However, reliable ML model development remains challenging because the currently available datasets are sparse, heterogeneous, and strongly dependent on local slag characteristics. Based on the critical findings of this review, future ML models for NCS systems should incorporate not only conventional mix-design parameters, but also slag-specific features such as oxide composition, amorphous content, crystallinity, cooling method, particle size distribution, activation method, replacement level, curing regime, and durability indicators. For example, the strong influence of particle fineness, cooling conditions, MgO phase stability in NS, and heavy-metal behaviour in LDS/ZS systems suggests that these variables are essential input parameters for predictive modelling. Integrating such material-specific descriptors into ML frameworks could support optimised mix design, performance prediction, durability assessment, and accelerated screening of suitable NCS for different cementitious applications.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This review critically evaluates the utilisation of NCS as partial replacements for cement and aggregates in cement-based materials. The findings demonstrate that the performance of NCS is highly dependent on their chemical composition, mineralogical characteristics, and processing history, rather than the slag type alone.

A key insight from this review is that most NCS exhibit limited intrinsic reactivity due to their predominantly crystalline nature, making them less suitable as standalone SCMs. However, they can still be effectively utilised either as aggregate replacements (e.g., CS, NS, LDS, and ZS) due to their favourable physical properties, or as SCMs in blended and activated systems (e.g., PS and LTS), where synergistic interactions compensate for their lower reactivity. The variability in reported performance across studies is primarily attributed to differences in particle size, cooling methods, replacement levels, and mix design parameters, highlighting the need for controlled and standardised evaluation. Conflicting results in the literature are not contradictory but condition-dependent. For instance, CS and NS consistently perform well as aggregates but show limited cementitious activity, whereas PS and LTS demonstrate good long-term pozzolanic behaviour but suffer from delayed early strength. LDS and ZS exhibit intermediate behaviour, where performance can be significantly improved through activation or blending strategies.

In a nutshell, NCS can serve as viable alternative materials in cement-based systems when their limitations are properly addressed through optimisation of mix design, processing, and activation. Their effective utilisation requires a shift from treating them as direct cement replacements to engineered components within multi-material systems. This approach enables both performance enhancement and environmental benefits, supporting the transition toward more sustainable and circular construction practices.
